episodes.171988: Thunderstorms repeatedly moved across portions of North Central and Northeastern Alabama, producing widespread rainfall amounts of 4 to more than 6 inches of rain. This produced both flash flooding and nuisance flooding in Marshall and Cullman Counties.
episodes.172380: A broad upper level trough combined with a weak front across western New York and a very moist air mass resulted in thunderstorms with heavy rain and flash flooding over western New York and the Southern Tier Labor Day afternoon and evening.
episodes.173142: A cold front stalled over southern New England causing very heavy rain and significant flash flooding before the front moved off the south coast during the evening. Rainfall amounts ranged from 7 to 11 inches in eastern Connecticut and the Providence metro area.
episodes.173143: A cold front stalled over southern New England causing very heavy rain and significant flash flooding before the front moved off the south coast during the evening. Rainfall amounts ranged from 7 to 11 inches in eastern Connecticut and the Providence metro area.

episodes.173170: Showers and thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall during the morning hours.
episodes.173185: Bands of locally slow-moving thunderstorms resulted in isolated instances of flash flooding. An elongated mid-level trough and associated closed low stretched through the middle Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys, helping to focus a stationary front across the region. Sufficient daytime heating helped generate moderate instability in the vicinity of the front. Where the slow-moving storms were locally focused near the front, isolated excessive rainfall occurred.
episodes.173213: A few showers and storms developed across eastern Mississippi during the afternoon and evening of September 4th. These storms were slow moving and brought heavy rain to the region.
episodes.173271: High moisture content under weak southerly steering flow produced heavy rainfall on already saturated grounds.
episodes.173369: Thunderstorms trained along a nearly stationary boundary crossing into northwest Pennsylvania during the evening hours of September 4th, taking advantage of a moisture-laden air mass. Instances of road flooding were observed in Mercer and Venango Counties.
episodes.173786: A thunderstorm produced a waterspout near Carolina Beach.
episodes.173876: On the 4th/5th, a new cold front drifted into Arkansas from the north and stalled. Surrounding the front, more hit and miss thunderstorms popped up on the 5th, and produced torrential rain in places. High temperatures were in the 80s to lower 90s.||During the afternoon, precipitation was concentrated from west central into central and southeast sections of the state. The heaviest downpours were between Little Rock (Pulaski County) and Benton (Saline County), with two to more than three inch totals reported. At Crystal Valley (Pulaski County), for example, 2.75 inches of liquid was measured.
episodes.174323: Scattered thunderstorms over Mohave County eventually merged into a complex which tracked southwest across much of the southern half of the county, producing widespread damaging winds and local flash flooding.
episodes.174324: A complex of thunderstorms over Mohave County, Arizona made it across the Colorado River and produced wind damage in Needles before dissipating.
episodes.174365: A stationary front draped over the area on September 5th and 6th allowed for the development of slow moving thunderstorms. These thunderstorms produced torrential rainfall in an environment with precipitable water values 1.8-2 inches. Anywhere from 2 to 4 inches of rainfall fell in a several hour period with some localized spots receiving close to 6 inches of rain.
episodes.174529: Isolated Severe Thunderstorms produced large hail in Callahan County.
episodes.174555: A quasi-stationary surface front and meandering mid-level cyclone continued to promote unsettled weather across the Ohio Valley on September 5th. During the morning hours, a slow-moving cluster of showers and thunderstorms across southwestern Indiana fed off of increasing diurnally-driven instability and a relatively moisture-rich environment, resulting in heavy rainfall across portions of Dubois County. In the community of Dubois, some minor flooding was observed, with rainfall totals of between 3 and 4 inches being reported in the vicinity of flood reports.
episodes.174556: A quasi-stationary surface front and weak mid-level cyclone continued to meander across the Ohio and Tennessee valleys on September 5th and 6th, providing localized convergence and broad forcing for ascent across central Kentucky. Temperatures in the low-to-mid 80s and dewpoints in the low 70s facilitated the development of around 2000 J/kg SBCAPE and Precipitable Water values approaching 2 inches during the afternoon and evening hours. The aforementioned thermodynamic and kinematic support was sufficient to promote widespread convection during the afternoon and evening hours on both September 5th and 6th. Relatively stagnant flow throughout most of the depth of the troposphere contributed to slow storm motion, resulting in localized flash flooding where the heaviest showers and thunderstorms developed and persisted. Multiple reports of flooding were observed in Taylor County on the afternoon of the 5th, with flooding being observed in Barren County on the afternoon of the 6th.
episodes.174626: A complex of thunderstorms over Mohave County, Arizona moved across the Colorado River and produced wind damage in Laughlin before dissipating.
episodes.174734: Heavy rain fell off and on throughout the first few days of September in the vicinity of a stalled frontal zone. A period of heavy rain during the morning of the 5th resulted in 1 to 2 inches in just a few hours across northern Oconee County, resulting in isolated flash flooding in the Chattooga River basin.
episodes.174769: Heavy rain fell off and on throughout the first few days of September in the vicinity of a stalled frontal zone. A period of heavy rain during the morning of the 5th resulted in 1 to 2.5 inches in just a few hours across southern Rabun County, resulting in isolated flash flooding in the Tallulah River basin.

events.narrative: All lanes of U.S. Highway 90 near the intersection of East Enterprise Blvd were closed in Macclenny due to flood water.

Waves estimated to be six feet high swept across Lake Havasu due to severe thunderstorm winds. Multiple boaters in distress were rescued from their crafts and from the water. One person was trapped under a capsized craft near the Havasu Landing Casino and drowned; that death is documented in the corresponding CA entry for this event.

events.narrative: A waterspout was observed near Carolina Beach.
In Southbridge, Dresser St. and Chapin St. were flooded and impassable due to a clogged storm drain in the area of Goddard at Depaul St. Relayed by amateur radio.
In Oxford, street flooding was reported on an unspecified road.
Camp Creek was out of its banks. Water was flowing across Camp Creek Road and entered a residence.

County comms reported flash flooding developed along tributaries of the Tallulah River in south central Rabun County ater 1 to 2.5 inches of rain fell over the course of a few hours. This was in addition to the 3 to 5 inches that had fallen over the area since the 2nd. Ramey Rd, Shady Ln, and Old Highway 441 were inundated by overflowing creeks.
In Webster, police reported that West Main St. (Rt. 197) at Mason Lane was closed due to flooding. Also, a portion of Worcester Rd (Rt. 12) was closed and impassable. Relayed by amateur radio.

County comms reported that a campground on Burrells Ford Rd at the Chattooga River was inundated with 2 to 3 feet of water and evacuated after 1 to 2 inches of rain fell during the morning of the 5th. This was on top of 3 to 5 inches of rain that had fallen across the area since the 2nd.
In Gloucester, the public reported flooding on an unspecified street.
In Milford, a portion of East Main St. was flooded and requiring DPW assistance. Relayed by amateur radio.
In the Chepachet section of Burrillville, Rt. 44 was underwater at Terry Ln. and Spring Grove Rd.

A school basement in the town of Dubois flooded, and local emergency services were requested to help remove water from the school. Rainfall totals of between 3 and 4 inches were observed in the vicinity of the flooding reports.
In Cumberland, Industrial Rd. was flooded. Relayed by amateur radio.

In Providence County, very heavy rain fell, eventually amounting to 7 to 10 inches. Approximately 6 inches fell in 2 hours leading to flash flooding. At 1:51 PM EDT Oregon St. at Whipple St. was closed.  At 2:05 PM EDT a car was stuck in street flooding on Valley St. at Eagle St. Cars were traveling in the wrong direction to avoid flooding on Pleasant Valley Parkway. At 2:26 PM EDT Dexter St. at Huntington Ave. was reported to be flooded and impassable. Relayed by amateur radio.
In North Providence, Library Rd. by Adams Library was flooded and impassable. Relayed by amateur radio.

In Cranston, at 2:02 PM EDT a car was stuck in street flooding on Fletcher Ave. Between 2:04 and 2:11 PM EDT multiple cars were stuck in street flooding on Atwood Ave. At 2:13 PM EDT Rt. 10 north at Union Ave was flooded and impassable with cars stuck in the flooding. Relayed by amateur radio.

In Providence, 7 to 10 inches of rain fell over the course of a few hours during the mid to late afternoon creating serious flash flooding. 8.31 inches of rain fell in the Elmwood section of the city and 6.89 in the College Hill section.  National news media showed aerial views of Interstate 95 which had become completely flooded and was closed in both directions. The snarled traffic lasted for multiple hours. Cars were reported to be stuck in the following locations: Webster Ave., Hamilton St., Cadillac Ave. at Melrose St. (water up to the windows), Narragansett Ave at Santiago St., Rugby St. at Thurbers Ave. Additional flooding and road closure reports included: Thackery St. at Melrose St., the underpass of Rt. 10 north at Westminster St., Hartford Ave. at Heath St., Smith St. at Gentian Ave., Exchange St., Pleasant Valley Parkway at Berlin St., Huntington Ave., Manton Ave. at Saban St., Elmwood Ave. ramp to Rt. 10, and Olneyville Square.  One block of Atwells Avenue was washed out. Many water rescues were necessary due to life-threatening situations.  All together, there were 3 injuries related to motor vehicle accidents during the storm and roughly 25 individuals rescued.  On Benevolent St. water invaded the 1st floor of a Brown University campus building. On Elmwood Ave. there was rapid flooding of a structure of unspecified type.  On Peace Street, there was a partial (25%) collapse of the roof of a vacant building, which was being redeveloped into a shopping plaza.  A total of 41 homes and businesses were flooded.  The West River overtopped its banks and flooded Charles Street and portions of Silver Spring Street in the evening.  The Woonasquatucket River crested at 6.07 ft. at 315 AM on September 7th, which was above the 5.5 ft. flood stage.  Many thanks to the Providence Emergency Management Agency for some of these details.
